of transplant patients display dyslipidemia, with increases in 
triglycerides, total cholesterol, and LDL. Increased oxida-
tion of LDL and possibly a decreased cardioprotective effect 
of HDL may also play a role.53 The causes of dyslipidemia 
are multifactorial, and include (1) genetic predisposition,
(2) pretransplant lipid levels, (3) certain immunosuppres-
sive agents (prednisone, cyclosporine, sirolimus), (4) other
medications (diuretics, beta blockers), (5) insulin resistance,
(6) obesity, (7) changes in proteinuria, and (8) impairment
in renal function. It is not clear how quickly these immuno-
suppressive agents alter lipoprotein metabolism. It is rec-
ommended that a lipid profile be measured during the first
six months posttransplant, at one year after transplantation, 
and yearly thereafter. Additional testing is recommended
when there are changes in immunosuppressive agents, graft 
function, or CVD risk.54, 55
